extracted.intended_audience: journal editors and publishers overseeing peer review (primarily scientific journals)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for editors and publishers on planning, piloting, implementing, communicating, and evaluating elements of open peer review (OPR) for journals and related publication venues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open identities
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors and reviewers are aware of each other's identity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defined as one of seven core traits of OPR. Reviews with open identities can seem more constructive in tone. Consider effects on reviewer recruitment and possible reluctance of reviewers; potential for retaliation against junior reviewers is a common concern (anecdotal). Options: pilot, make optional, opt-in/out, make open identities default with opt-out, or publish reviewer names only alongside final article. Enable credit by linking reviewer names to persistent identifiers (e.g., ORCID) and services like Publons. Devise invitation text explaining pros/cons and be prepared to offer negotiation (e.g., more time) to reticent reviewers. Have workflows to manage negative interactions and monitor whether open identities change review tone or recruitment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Review reports (full reports or summaries) are published alongside the relevant article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Benefits: makes invisible but useful scholarly information available; increases transparency, accountability and potential reviewer credit by linking to ORCID/Publons. Best-practice advice (Beck et al. 2018) recommends assigning individual DOIs to reports and three implementation routes: (1) attach peer review materials as single or multiple PDFs with mechanism for JATS XML tagging; (2) append review materials within full text as a sub-article component in XML; (3) publish peer review materials as full-text XML 'articles' or 'commentaries' that link bidirectionally to the main article — option 3 is best practice though option 1 is most pragmatic. Machine-readable metadata should accompany content. Be aware of costs, editorial time to prepare/redact reports, policy on confidential messages to editors, version management, and processes for handling derogatory/defamatory content; add disclaimers if redactions occur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open participation
rubrics_metrics.description: The wider community is able to contribute to the review process (pre- or post-publication).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Can allow any interested community members (or require credentials) to contribute full reviews or shorter comments. Decide whether anonymous commenting is allowed or whether identity/affiliation is required; some indexing services require named individuals. Open participation often has low uptake and is best used as a complement to invited peer review. Foster uptake via outreach to potential commentators, social media amplification, or mediation. Consider platform decisions (publisher site vs third-party) and moderation policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open interaction
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct reciprocal discussion between author(s) and reviewers, and/or between reviewers, is allowed and encouraged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enables editors and reviewers to work with authors to improve manuscripts via interaction. Decide which workflow to enable (pre-publication reviewer-reviewer interaction, consultative review, or interactive collaboration involving authors/reviewers/editors). Examples: EMBO Journal and eLife enable pre-publication interaction; Frontiers includes an interactive collaboration stage. Be alert to editorial workload implications: may increase some tasks but reduce others (e.g., eLife reports more upfront work but less later). Define moderation and facilitation roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open pre-review manuscripts
rubrics_metrics.description: Manuscripts are made immediately available (e.g., via preprint servers) in advance of formal peer review procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supports faster dissemination, priority claims, and community commenting; can reduce repeated review cycles across journals. Consider relationships between preprints and journal processes, potential versioning issues, and how to link subsequent peer reviews/reports to preprint versions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open final version commenting
rubrics_metrics.description: Review or commenting on final 'version of record' publications is enabled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allows post-publication critique and continued quality assurance of the published record. Decide policies for moderation, linking comments to article versions, and whether to integrate comments into article metadata or as separate items. Consider indexing and discoverability implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open platforms (decoupled review)
rubrics_metrics.description: Review is facilitated by a different organisational entity than the venue of publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Separating review platforms from publication venues supports review portability and decoupling. Consider platform interoperability, metadata/linking between review and publication, and possible partnerships with third-party OPR services as plug-ins to existing workflows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide what you would like to achieve with OPR (Set goals)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any journal editor or publisher wishing to implement some form of OPR should first do their homework: what do you want to achieve? How? For which reasons? Which aspects of peer review do you want to improve?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be clear on primary goals (e.g., increase transparency, give credit to reviewers, enable participation, speed up review). Relate goals to specific OPR elements and build a provisional strategic plan. Study existing models, literature, and industry examples. Recognise resource/time commitments vary by element (e.g., disclosing names is easier than publishing full peer review histories).

rubrics_metrics.name: Acquaint yourself with differences between OPR elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Familiarise yourself with the different elements of open peer review and how they differ (seven-core-trait taxonomy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read widely and consult primers and literature. Understand pros and cons for each trait and how combinations create different configurations; use industry examples and additional readings (e.g., Additional file 1). This knowledge helps map goals to feasible elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide which OPR elements to implement
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose specific elements of openness to include based on goals and feasibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refine plans by studying existing models, using industry contacts, and considering resource/time costs. Prioritise elements given technical feasibility and community readiness. Consider pilots or phased approaches where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be conscious of, and sensitive to, community differences
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognise that perceptions and willingness to adopt OPR vary across disciplines and communities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some disciplines have traditions (e.g., double-blind) and may resist openness; consider starting with disciplines more open to OPR or with journals already using OPR. For broad-scope journals, be mindful of interdisciplinary tensions when selecting elements to pilot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider surveying community opinions
rubrics_metrics.description: Gauge attitudes towards OPR by surveying or interviewing your communities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use surveys for close-knit or society journals; complement with qualitative interviews of stakeholders with strong opinions. Tailor approaches to journal/community context to gather actionable feedback before implementing changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communicate your goal with stakeholders and the research community
rubrics_metrics.description: Engage editorial boards, reviewers and authors early to 'sell' benefits and gather buy-in.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use editorials, webinars, infographics, blog posts to articulate decisions and justify them. Include requests for community feedback in announcements. Identify a committed Editor and 'open champions' to drive discussions and recruitment. Make policies easily findable on journal webpages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess technological feasibility of various options
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether editorial office, production and publication systems can support chosen OPR elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small publishers using open-source systems vs large publishers on major manuscript handling services may have differing capabilities. Some OPR elements require significant system configuration or development; determine current system support and whether technical staff or vendor development is needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess the costs of various options
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify initial development and ongoing support costs for OPR options.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of lack of infrastructure and potential need for custom development, editorial staff time, and ongoing maintenance. Consider cost-sharing partnerships with other publishers or using platforms offering OPR functionality. Recognise different implementation approaches vary in elegance and cost (manual compilation vs automated XML workflows).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider workaround options for piloting
rubrics_metrics.description: When experimenting, consider starting with small-scale or manual workarounds rather than full platform integration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Workarounds may have sub-optimal user experience and could inhibit uptake; weigh trade-offs. Third-party OPR platforms can act as plug-ins to existing workflows for pilot studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set priorities and consider a phased approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Be pragmatic: choose priorities, avoid changing too many things at once, and phase implementation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A phased approach helps maintain traction and community buy-in and makes it easier to assess each innovation's success. Prioritise elements that communities are receptive to and be prepared to compromise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider making options optional or piloting them first
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce controversial elements as optional or via pilot programs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Optional or pilot approaches allow signalling support while allowing opt-out. Note default settings (opt-in vs opt-out) significantly affect participation. Pair pilots with participant surveys and ex ante performance indicators to inform final decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engage the community, especially via 'open champions'
rubrics_metrics.description: Find and use enthusiastic researchers to advocate for OPR among peers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recruit open champions from initial community consultations to advocate and model behaviour. Use their voices in communications to help sell the concept and increase uptake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware that communication is key and terminology is important
rubrics_metrics.description: Clear, accessible communication about OPR decisions, benefits and risks is essential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publish clear policies, use plain language, and provide justifications. Use multiple channels (editorials, webinars, FAQs) to ensure authors and reviewers understand processes and implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Have a clear framework for assessing success
rubrics_metrics.description: Define how you will measure whether OPR is meeting goals before implementation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide which metrics (e.g., review quality, difficulty finding reviewers, review times, consultation/re-use of open reports) will be measured, on which populations, and over what timescale. Systematically collect data and consider partnering with peer review researchers to enable rigorous analyses. Establish ex ante quantifiable measures and performance indicators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept that change takes time, but adjust if necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Cultural change is slow; persist but be ready to revise if evidence shows problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be patient with uptake but monitor indicators; if things are not working, revisit phased approaches and optionality. Balance ethical aims (transparency/accountability) against practical outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Share your results with the community
rubrics_metrics.description: Report on implementation outcomes and lessons learned to inform others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide updates to authors, reviewers, editors and staff; consider writing up findings as scientific studies or partnering with researchers to enable external analysis. Sharing fills evidence gaps about OPR efficacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Devise strategies to compensate for reviewer recruitment challenges under open identities
rubrics_metrics.description: Create tailored communications and incentives to secure reviewers for open-identity review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare standard invitation and follow-up texts explaining the process and its pros/cons. Be ready to negotiate with potential reviewers (e.g., offer more time). Monitor whether open identities make reviewer recruitment harder and adapt strategies accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be alert to possible negative interactions and have a workflow for dealing with them
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepare policies and procedures to handle conflicts, retaliation concerns, defamatory or inflammatory language, and reviewer safety issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set clear processes for reviewers to raise concerns, have editorial policies for handling derogatory/defamatory remarks and redactions, and consider disclaimers for omitted confidential communications. Monitor evidence about negative consequences and contribute data to the evidence base.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enable credit (link reviewer contributions to persistent identifiers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use ORCID or similar to connect reviewer identities and published reports for credit and career evaluation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assign persistent identifiers to reviewers and consider integrations with Publons or similar services. This is a best practice to make review work citable, discoverable and creditable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider piloting or making open identities optional
rubrics_metrics.description: Because open identities are controversial, offer pilots or opt-in/opt-out choices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Options include opt-in, opt-out defaults, pilots, publishing names only with the final article, or maintaining blind review but publishing names later. Be mindful that selection effects may bias outcomes (e.g., lenient reviewers more likely to opt in).

rubrics_metrics.name: Meet industry best-practice for publishing review reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt emerging best practices for publishing peer review materials (e.g., assigning DOIs, machine-readable metadata, XML approaches).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow Beck et al. (2018) recommendations: prefer publishing reports as full-text XML articles linking bidirectionally to main article (best practice), but pragmatic options include attaching PDFs. Ensure machine-readable metadata and consider DOIs per report to make them citable and discoverable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware of potential challenges in publishing reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognise editorial time, redaction needs, confidentiality issues, version management and resource costs in publishing review reports.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect editorial labor (e.g., 20–40 minutes per article for preparation/redaction). Publish clear policies on handling derogatory/defamatory content and confidential messages to editors. Implement coherent version management and consider disclaimers where confidential comments are omitted. Plan for development or ongoing cost barriers, especially for smaller publishers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide who can comment for open participation
rubrics_metrics.description: Set policy on whether comments are open to anybody (anonymous or registered) or restricted to identified/credentialed individuals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Options vary by publisher (e.g., Copernicus requires identity for commentators; MDPI relaxed registration requirement). Consider indexing requirements which may need named individuals and affiliations. Balance openness with quality and indexing concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider how to foster uptake for open participation
rubrics_metrics.description: Plan strategies to increase community engagement in open participation processes, recognising low baseline participation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complement open participation with solicited peer review, mediate discussions, reach out directly to potential commentators, publicise via social media, and highlight conversations to entice engagement. Treat open participation as complementary rather than a replacement for invited review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide which workflow to enable for open interaction
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose the specific interaction workflow among authors, reviewers and editors for your journal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Options include reviewer-reviewer pre-publication interaction, consultative review to draft consensus decisions, and interactive collaboration stages including authors and editors. Study models (EMBO, eLife, Frontiers) and define facilitation/moderation roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be alert to how open interaction may affect editorial workloads
rubrics_metrics.description: Anticipate changes to editorial labor when enabling interaction between actors in the review process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interactive processes may increase upfront workload (e.g., consultations, drafting consensus letters) but can save time later (e.g., eLife's approach). Monitor workload impacts and resource requirements during pilot phases.
